newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia's CBA battles home mortgage price war.
newsitem.headline: Australia's CBA battles home mortgage price war.

text.p: The Commonwealth Bank of Australia (CBA) announced an 8.0 percent rise in annual profits on Wednesday, but warned margin and cost pressures would be the fallout from a home mortgage price war.
Offsetting a bearish profit outlook, CBA announced a A$650 million (US$484 million) share buy-back and an information technology alliance with U.S. technology group Electronic Data Systems Inc.
The bank said the technology deal would generate A$5.0 billion in revenue in 10 years.

CBA Managing Director David Murray said the current year to June 30, 1998, would test profits as the lagged effect of a 120 basis point squeeze in home loan margins rolled through to the bank's bottom line.

"There's a hangover effect from the reduction in home loan margins and we're making further investments for our financial services integration which will reflect in operating expenses," Murray told a news conference.

"We still have labour unit costs rising, so taken overall, it's going to be a very difficult year to make significant gains, with margin pressure and with some ongoing investments which we think are pretty good for the future," Murray said.
CBA's net profit after tax, but before abnormals for the year to June 30, rose eight percent to A$1.206 billion, just above the median forecast by analysts of a profit of A$1.189 billion.
However, net profit after abnormals fell four percent to A$1.078 billion after an abnormal post-tax loss of A$128 million for a planned technology restructuring.
CBA increased its final dividend to 57 cents from 52 cents.

But the results included an increase in CBA's cost to income ratio in the second half to 62 percent from 60 percent in the first half and CBA's group net interest margin fell to 3.41 percent from 4.00 percent over the year.
Higher wages and over A$100 million in costs to fix bugs associated with the Year 2000 Millenium would add to the pressure on the bank's costs in the coming year, Murray added.
Bad and doubtful debt expenses were also set to rise again as the debt cycle appeared to have troughed, Murray said.
"We are running out of some fairly juicy write-back opportunities that we've had over the last few years and I really do think this year that it might have hit rock bottom."
CBA's charge for bad and doubtful debts fell to A$98 million in 1996/97 from A$113 million a year earlier.
The bank said the buy-back would be carried out later this year to return excess capital.

CBA said the formation of the partnership with EDS would cut costs and improve its systems. CBA said it would take a 35 percent stake in EDS Australia and that the alliance was expected to have a life of at least 10 years.
"The proposed partnership will be one of the world's largest IT (information technology) alliances within the financial services industry," CBA said.
Murray said the details on expected cost savings to flow from the alliance and the price of the 35 percent stake had yet to be finalised.
All IT functions are to be included in the partnership.
CBA's shares were down 12 cents at A$16.25 at 3.00 p.m. (0500 GMT) in a weak market overall.
